content.text: Dubai’s modern journey started with pearl diving and evolved through regional trade, accelerating in the 1960s with the discovery of oil. Since then, Dubai has expanded into tourism, aviation, logistics, real estate, and financial services. Today, its next economic pivot is artificial intelligence (AI), not as a pilot experiment, but as an operational layer embedded across sectors.As of July 2025, Dubai ranks among the top 10 AI cities globally, according to Counterpoint Research’s 2025 Global AI Cities Index, a study assessing AI adoption via public- and private-sector initiatives, compute infrastructure, startup ecosystems, and education. Government institutions have been mandated to adopt AI and train officials in its use. Alongside the UAE National AI Strategy that aims to position the UAE as a global AI leader by 2031, Dubai has also created its own roadmap to invite AI companies and talent while enhancing the quality of life through technology. At the heart of this roadmap is the transition from generative AI experimentation to agentic AI execution. Generative (Gen) AI systems create content, insights, and decision-support tools, automating analysis, drafting, and data interpretation. Agentic AI, by contrast, goes a step further: it executes workflows autonomously, coordinates across systems, and takes action in real time within defined governance frameworks. Dubai’s ambition lies not just in deploying AI tools, but in embedding autonomous systems into aviation, logistics, utilities, and city management.In its Annual Results (2025) report, Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) revealed its position as one of the region’s largest innovation-focused communities, now home to 1677 AI and fintech companies.Compute infrastructure in the UAE comes from the best in the global game. It has one of the highest concentrations of data centres in the region (Oracle, IBM, Amazon, and Microsoft), while local companies, such as du, from Emirates Integrated Telecommunications Company (EITC), and etisalat by e&, develop sovereign cloud functionality, which are a critical need for handling sensitive financial and government data. Sandboxing facilities allow businesses to test new technology in controlled environments. For instance, the DIFC Innovation Hub provides regulatory sandboxing and access to institutional partners. Dubai AI Campus offers education programmes alongside subsidised commercial licensing. Within the Dubai Future Foundation ecosystem, startups can test AI solutions in controlled, real-world environments while coordinating directly with regulators. ET SpotlightFrom labs to live environmentsHowever, the defining shift is visible in how AI is moving from labs to live environments. At Dubai Airports, biometric smart gate systems using facial recognition technology have streamlined passenger processing at Dubai International Airport. Dubai Electricity and Water Authority deploys AI-driven predictive analytics to forecast electricity and water demand across its smart grid infrastructure. In logistics, DP World has integrated intelligent systems to optimise routing, reduce downtime, and improve asset utilisation across its port operations. These are not pilot initiatives; they represent AI embedded within live operational systems. Companies such as Net0, co-founded by Sofia Fominova, have also expanded from the UK into the Dubai market, providing AI infrastructure to governments and enterprises. “We have benefited significantly from Dubai’s innovation ecosystem”, says Fominova. “In particular, we participated in the Dubai Future Foundation and the Dubai Centre for Artificial Intelligence Accelerator programmes.”Another avenue of opportunity that entrepreneurs are tapping into is that of AI advisory, especially as governments and enterprises seek digital transformation. “Leadership teams, including CEOs, boards, and CIOs, sometimes either don’t know where to start with AI or struggle to extract value from it”, says Vijay Jaswal, Founder of Kudo Advisory. This is where advisory service firms step in to provide end-to-end strategy, governance, value identification, and solution delivery. For Indian AI startups and advisory firms, Dubai’s regulated sandbox environments and access to enterprise clients across aviation, logistics, and financial services shorten the path from product development to commercial deployment.Funding is also expanding. A recent Magnitt report indicates that AI startup funding in MENA rose by 22% in 2025, with more than 60% of AI capital directed towards the UAE. The DIFC Innovation Hub and AI Campus together raised over $4.5 billion. Venture firms are active, but so too are family offices. Younger generations of wealthy families are seeing value in directing funds to AI and related technologies, according to Dr Bhaskar Dasgupta, Chairman of APEX Group.However, Dubai recognises that AI can only grow so much with foreign companies entering the market. Real growth comes when talent develops locally. The Dubai Future Foundation plays a pivotal role here in bridging public and private innovation. Its ‘One Million Prompters’ initiative aims to train one million individuals in prompt engineering over several years.Visa liberalisation, including long-term Golden Visas, further enables Dubai to attract global engineers, founders, and researchers. The result is that human capital in Dubai is propped up by local upskilling and international talent acquisition.Alongside capability is the ever-evolving regulatory landscape. According to Jaswal, “In Dubai, regulation doesn’t block AI but shapes how it’s built, hosted, and governed.” While there is no standalone federal AI law, regulation is far from absent. The UAE’s Personal Data Protection Law and DIFC’s Data Protection Law govern data privacy, cross-border transfers, and accountability frameworks. DIFC’s sandbox model allows controlled experimentation under supervisory oversight.That’s one part of the AI roadmap: driving companies and talent into Dubai. The second part is enhancing the quality of life. “I don’t have to take my passport out at Dubai International Airport anymore’, notes Jaswal, ‘thanks to the smart gates and tunnels.” According to him, everyday results such as Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (DEWA) predicting energy usage, and traffic lights adjusting to congestion using AI, are some examples of how AI can quietly enhance the quality of life. With all of these developments underway, Dubai’s AI story is no longer confined to pilot projects or accelerator programmes. The shift now is towards scale: moving from experimentation to embedded, enterprise-grade systems operating across critical infrastructure.And if Dubai’s earlier growth phases were built on geography and hydrocarbons, this next chapter is increasingly defined by code, written, deployed, and executed at scale.This article is authored by Amandeep Kaur Ahuja.
